newsitem.title: USA: U.S. moves against Argentina in patent dispute.
newsitem.headline: U.S. moves against Argentina in patent dispute.

text.p: The United States said Wednesday it would withdraw half of Argentina's duty-free trade benefits because Argentine laws failed to protect the intellectual property rights of U.S. drug companies.
U.S. Trade Representative-designate Charlene Barshefsky said the action would affect about $260 million worth of Argentine exports to the United States.
"We have seen some encouraging efforts on the part of the (President Carlos) Menem administration to establish modern intellectual property protection in Argentina," Barshefsky said in a statement.
"However, Argentina's resulting patent law and the new legislation designed to protect test registration data fall short of this objective and fail to meet international standards", she said.
President Clinton advised Menem of his decision in a letter made public on Tuesday in Buenos Aires.
Argentine officials played down the effect of the U.S. action on exports and local newspapers reported the move would cost the country between $10 million and $20 million a year.
Barshefsky said the new Argentine patent laws passed in 1995 and 1996 still allow Argentina's pharmaceutical companies to freely copy drugs developed by U.S. firms.
The United States has been pressing Argentina for years to reform its laws on intellectual property rights, which until 1995 set no restrictions on copying foreign drug patents.
The U.S. pharmaceutical industry, which long called for action against Argentina, says that its companies lose around $500 million every year due to patent "piracy" in Argentina.

Menem, who has sought to strengthen Argentina's diplomatic ties with Washington, proposed legislation that would have pleased the United States, but his bills were blocked or watered down by the Argentine Congress.
In her statement, Barshefsky said, "Argentine pharmaceutical interests continue to work aggressively to frustrate our efforts to achieve improved intellectual property protection in other countries".

Argentina's Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella said on Monday that the United States was planning actions that would group Argentina with nations it does not usually like to associate with, but that they would be ineffectual.
"It puts us in a pestilent category (of nations), but it's neither here nor there to us," Di Tella told reporters.

The U.S. Trade Representative's statement added that the final list of Argentine products to be excluded from Washington's system of duty-free trade preferences will be published "on or about March 1".
A spokesman for the U.S. Trade Representative said the sanctions would be imposed on manufactured goods but not raw commodities.
